title: Road Signs
summary: How to read any sign from its shape and color, and what the most-tested regulatory, warning, school, railroad, work-zone and guide signs mean.

sections.heading: Shape and color tell you the message

blocks.text: Signs come in three main groups. Regulatory signs tell you what the law requires. Warning signs tell you about a hazard ahead. Guide signs tell you where you are and how to reach a place. You can often know a sign's message from its shape and color before you can read it.

rows: STOP. No other sign uses this shape.
Regulatory: rules such as speed limits and lane use.
Warning: a hazard or change in the road ahead.
Warnings about schools, pedestrians, bicyclists and playgrounds.
Incident ahead, such as a crash or other unplanned event.
Directions, distances, exits and route guidance.
Motorist services such as gas, food, lodging and hospitals.
Parks, recreation and scenic or historic places.

blocks.text: A red circle with a slash through a symbol always means that action is not allowed, such as NO LEFT TURN or NO U-TURN.

items: STOP: come to a complete stop at the stop line. If there is no line, stop before the crosswalk; if there is no crosswalk, stop before the intersection. Yield to pedestrians and cross traffic, then go when it is safe.
ALL-WAY plaque under a STOP sign: every approach must stop. The first vehicle to stop goes first. If two arrive together, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.
YIELD: slow down and be ready to stop. Let vehicles, bicyclists and pedestrians on the other road go first. You do not have to stop if the way is clear.
DO NOT ENTER: you may not enter from this direction, such as the wrong end of a one-way street or a freeway exit ramp.
WRONG WAY: you are driving against traffic. Pull out of the traffic path and turn around as soon as it is safe.

blocks.text: Plaques add to the sign above them. ALL WAY under a STOP sign means every approach stops. TO ONCOMING TRAFFIC under a YIELD sign means you must yield to traffic coming toward you, as at a one-lane bridge.
A STOP sign means a full stop every time, even when no one is coming. A rolling stop is a violation.
These white, black and red signs are law, not advice. Ignoring them can earn you a ticket.

items: Turn prohibitions: NO RIGHT TURN, NO LEFT TURN, NO U-TURN, NO U-TURN OR LEFT TURN and NO TURNS mean exactly that, even when no traffic is coming. A straight arrow with a slash means you may not go straight; you must turn.
NO TURN ON RED: wait for a green light or green arrow before turning.
ONE WAY: traffic moves only in the direction of the arrow.
KEEP RIGHT: pass to the right of the island or obstacle ahead.
DO NOT BLOCK INTERSECTION: do not enter unless there is room for your whole car on the far side.

blocks.text: Lane-use signs tell you which way each lane must go. Get into the right lane early.

items: LEFT TURN ONLY or RIGHT TURN ONLY: vehicles in that lane must turn that way.
RIGHT LANE MUST TURN RIGHT: move out of that lane early if you want to go straight.
Center lane two-way left turn only: the center lane is for left turns by traffic from both directions, never for passing.
HOV or carpool lane: only for vehicles carrying at least the posted number of people during the posted hours.
SPEED LIMIT: the most you may drive in good conditions. Drive slower when weather, traffic or the road calls for it.
A sign with a maximum and a minimum speed: in normal conditions, stay between the two numbers.
Plaques under a speed limit sign can set a lower limit for trucks or at night.
DO NOT PASS marks a no-passing zone; PASS WITH CARE marks where it ends.
SLOWER TRAFFIC KEEP RIGHT and KEEP RIGHT EXCEPT TO PASS: use the right lane unless you are passing.

blocks.text: Speed limits themselves, and the default limits on roads with no signs, are set by each state. Check your State Cheat Sheet.
Yellow diamond warning signs tell you to slow down and get ready for what is ahead.

items: Turn signs show a sharp bend; curve signs show a gentler one. Slow down before you reach it.
Reverse turn or reverse curve: the road bends one way, then back the other way.
Winding road: three or more curves in a row.
A number inside or under a warning sign is the advisory speed: the speed advised for that curve or ramp in good conditions. Go slower in rain, snow or at night.
Large arrows and chevrons on the outside of a sharp curve point the way the road turns.
A two-headed arrow across the end of a road means you cannot go straight; turn left or right.
Crossroad and side road: other vehicles may enter or cross ahead.
T intersection: your road ends; be ready to turn left or right.
Y intersection: the road splits; bear left or right.
The yellow pennant no-passing sign is placed on the left side of the road where the no-passing zone begins.
The five-sided school sign warns that a school or school crossing is near. Slow down and watch for children.
With a small arrow plaque pointing down at an angle, it marks the school crosswalk itself. Yield to anyone crossing.
SCHOOL BUS STOP AHEAD: a bus may be stopped to load or unload children.
A school speed limit applies when the sign's condition is met, such as when lights are flashing or children are present. The limit and hours vary by state; see your State Cheat Sheet.
A round yellow sign with an X and RR warns of a railroad crossing ahead. The same X and RR are often painted on the road.
The white crossbuck marks the crossing itself. Treat it like a yield sign for trains: slow down, look and listen both ways, and stop if a train is coming.
A plaque under the crossbuck shows the number of tracks. After one train passes, watch for a second one on another track.
Flashing red lights or lowered gates mean stop. Do not go until the gates are fully up and the lights stop.

blocks.text: Orange signs mark construction and maintenance work: lane closings, lane shifts, flaggers, uneven pavement and detours. Slow down, keep extra space, and watch for workers and equipment, even if no lower speed is posted.

items: Obey a flagger's signals just as you would a sign.
Many states raise fines in work zones. A FINES DOUBLE plaque tells you the zone has higher fines; check your State Cheat Sheet for your state's rule.
ROAD CLOSED means do not drive past the sign. Follow the detour.
Fluorescent pink signs warn of a crash or other unplanned incident ahead. Slow down and watch for stopped traffic and emergency crews.

blocks.text: An orange triangle with a red border on the back of a vehicle means it moves slowly, usually 25 mph or less. Farm equipment and horse-drawn buggies use it. Slow down early and pass only when it is safe and legal.

items: Green signs give directions, distances and exit information. A yellow EXIT ONLY panel means the lane under it leaves the highway.
Blue signs point to services such as gas, food, lodging, rest areas and hospitals.
Brown signs point to parks, recreation areas and scenic or historic sites.
Route markers show the highway number. Interstate signs are red, white and blue shields; U.S. routes use a white shield; state routes use shapes each state chooses.
On interstates, odd numbers generally run north-south and even numbers run east-west.
Mile markers show your location along a highway and help you report a crash or breakdown. In many states, exit numbers match the nearest mile marker.

blocks.text: When you call for help on a highway, give the route, your direction and the nearest mile marker or exit number.

keyPoints: Octagon means STOP; a downward triangle means YIELD. No other signs use these shapes.
Red and white or black and white signs are rules you must obey; a red circle with a slash means not allowed.
Yellow diamonds warn of hazards; the number on a warning sign is an advisory speed for good conditions.
A pennant marks the start of a no-passing zone; a pentagon marks a school zone or crossing.
A round yellow sign means a railroad crossing ahead; the crossbuck means yield to trains.
Orange means work zone: slow down and obey flaggers.
Green guides, blue shows services, brown shows recreation.
Speed limits, school-zone limits and work-zone fines vary by state; check your State Cheat Sheet.
